analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on offshore tax havens and abusive tax shelters used to dodge federal taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it much harder to hide money in offshore tax havens and to sell artificial tax shelters. It would have let the IRS presume that money moving through accounts in secrecy jurisdictions is taxable income unless the taxpayer proves otherwise, extended the time limit for auditing offshore deals, required banks and financial institutions to report who really owns foreign accounts, and imposed tough new penalties on the promoters and advisors who sell these schemes. The bill was referred to three House committees, was sent to one subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who effectively cover the taxes that wealthy individuals and corporations avoid through offshore structures. Honest businesses that compete against entities using secrecy jurisdictions would also face fairer competition, and the IRS would gain stronger tools and more time to pursue offshore evasion.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a legal presumption that a person who controls or receives money through an entity or account in an offshore secrecy jurisdiction controls it, and that amounts received from or paid to such accounts are taxable income — rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence [S3].

It gives the IRS six years instead of the usual period to audit returns involving offshore secrecy jurisdictions, and authorizes special measures — such as cutting off U.S. correspondent accounts and card transactions — against foreign banks and jurisdictions that impede U.S. tax enforcement [S3].

It requires financial institutions to report the true U.S. owners of foreign accounts and offshore entities, requires hedge funds and private equity funds to run anti-money-laundering programs, and imposes penalties of up to $1 million for knowingly failing to disclose offshore holdings [S3].

It raises penalties for promoters of abusive tax shelters to as much as 150 percent of their income from the activity, bans tax advisors' contingent-fee deals tied to tax savings, blocks patents on tax-avoidance techniques, and denies tax deductions for fines and penalties [S3].
It writes the economic substance doctrine into law and adds a 40 percent penalty on underpayments from transactions that lack real business purpose, with a lower 20 percent rate if disclosed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy individuals and companies that use offshore secrecy jurisdictions to shield income, along with the financial industry that profits from serving them: offshore banks and trust companies, hedge funds and private equity funds facing new anti-money-laundering rules, banks and brokerages facing new exams, and tax advisors who sell shelter opinions or charge fees contingent on tax savings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore finance, hedge funds, and tax advisors

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is real: banks, securities firms, and formation agents would face new reporting duties, and hedge funds and private equity funds would be required to build anti-money-laundering programs and file suspicious activity reports within 180 days of enactment, costs that regulated firms typically pass on to customers [S3].

The presumptions are broad: any U.S. person connected to an entity or account in one of 34 listed jurisdictions — including Hong Kong, Singapore, Cyprus, and Latvia — would be presumed to control it and to have taxable income from it, and could rebut the presumption only with clear and convincing evidence, which could entangle legitimate cross-border business and family arrangements [S3].

Some might lose access to legitimate offshore structures: the bill lets the Treasury Secretary cut off U.S. correspondent accounts and card transactions with jurisdictions or banks deemed to impede tax enforcement, a power whose breadth would depend on how it is used [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff favors stronger enforcement: offshore secrecy costs the Treasury revenue that other taxpayers ultimately make up, and the bill targets that directly. The cost side is compliance expense for financial firms and the risk that broad presumptions sweep in legitimate transactions, which the bill partially addresses by letting regulators exempt classes of transactions and by requiring clear and convincing evidence to overcome — but not eliminate — those concerns.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees for the rest of the two-year Congress and expired without any committee vote or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act on May 3, 2007 [S1].
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Financial Services and Judiciary Committees [S5].
On June 4, 2007, a portion of the bill was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill had 47 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
No committee reported the bill and no chamber ever voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy individuals and companies using offshore tax havens, and the banks, hedge funds, and tax advisors that profit from offshore secrecy and shelter sales, are better off because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Users of offshore havens and their advisors

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act in the House.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup and never reported the bill out.

against.name: Financial Services and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no further action beyond an initial subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican support appears in the record; since the bill never reached a vote, opposition was never formally recorded.

industries.industry: Offshore financial services (banks, trust companies, and formation agents in secrecy jurisdictions)
industries.note: The bill names 34 secrecy jurisdictions, presumes income and control for their entities and accounts, and lets Treasury cut off their U.S. correspondent accounts and card access. Their business model depends on the secrecy the bill targets [S3].

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: They would face a mandatory anti-money-laundering rule and suspicious activity reporting within 180 days of enactment. Their cost is the public's gain in enforcement visibility [S3].

Contingent fees tied to tax savings would be banned, offshore opinions could no longer shield clients from penalties, opinion standards would tighten, and promotion penalties could reach 150 percent of the income from the activity [S3].

They would have to report foreign accounts and offshore entities they open for U.S. clients, and banking regulators and the SEC would develop exams to detect shelter promotion. Additional compliance costs, ultimately borne by customers [S3].
